title: Same Job, Lower Pay? Wage Gaps between Renewable and Non-Renewable Electric Power Generation in the United States, 2021-2025
paper_claim: Between May 2021 and May 2025, U.S. renewable electricity generation industries paid about 11.5 percent less per hour than fossil fuel and nuclear generation for workers in the same detailed occupation; the gap was concentrated in solar, wind, geothermal and biomass (not hydroelectric) generation and in plant-operations and maintenance occupations, and it did not narrow while renewable generation employment doubled.
claim_change_note: Relative to the Phase 1 framing, the final claim adds that composition does not explain the gap (H2 not supported) and that the gap did not narrow (H5 not supported).

publication_readiness.contribution_sentence: Using five years of OEWS industry-by-occupation wage cells, we show that the same occupations pay roughly 11-12 percent less in U.S. renewable generation than in fossil and nuclear generation, that this gap is a within-occupation pay difference rather than an occupational-mix artifact, and that it persisted through the 2021-2025 renewable buildout.
publication_readiness.novelty_claim: First within-occupation, source-by-source comparison of renewable and non-renewable generation wages inside one industry, tracked through the IRA period; reconciles economy-wide green-premium findings with legacy-premium evidence for energy-transition policy readers of Energy Policy.
publication_readiness.target_journal_fit: Energy Policy publishes transparent empirical evidence on energy-transition labor outcomes; this paper gives policy-relevant, source-specific wage comparisons for just-transition and labor-standards debates.

contribution_stack.claim_text: Same-occupation renewable wage gap of about 11.5% inside U.S. power generation, 2021-2025.
The gap is technology- and occupation-specific: hydro at parity, nuclear premium, largest gaps for plant-operations workers.
No narrowing during a period of rapid renewable expansion and new labor standards.
Reconciles green-premium and legacy-premium literatures by locating the energy-transition wage penalty in establishment wage-setting rather than occupational composition.

hypothesis_resolution.manuscript_implication: Headline: renewable industries pay about 11.5% less for the same occupation and year; robust to weighting, outcome, sample, classification and clustering.

Occupational composition does not explain the raw gap; renewable occupational mix slightly favors higher pay. Report as a substantive finding: the gap is a within-occupation pay difference plus occupations unique to one group.

Nuclear pays about 12% more than fossil; hydro is statistically indistinguishable from fossil; solar, wind, geothermal and biomass pay less. Geothermal rests on 26 identifying cells and is described as imprecise.

Gap largest in production/transportation (about -18%) and construction/installation/maintenance/repair (about -14%), smallest in professional/technical (about -2%, n.s.); joint test rejects equal gaps. Lower-tail (P10) gap larger than upper-tail (P90) gap.
No narrowing: within-occupation gap -11% in 2021 and -13% in 2025; trend near zero and not significant. Framed under OEWS panel smoothing; no policy attribution.
